text: It's 1789. You're King Louis XVI of France. The palace shines, but the people are hungry and angry. Your money chest is empty. What's your move?

answers.text: Tell the wealthy nobles and church to start paying taxes too.

pros: Feels fair to the common people.
cons: Rich elites will resist strongly.

answers.text: Raise taxes on the common folk again.

pros: Fast way to refill the treasury.
cons: Already struggling people may explode in anger.

answers.text: Borrow money from foreign lenders and hope you can pay later.

pros: Gives quick relief without new taxes.
cons: Piles up debt for the future.

answers.text: Cut palace spending and put on public events to calm the crowd.

pros: Shows you care about the people's struggles.
cons: Doesn't fix the deep money shortage.

text: It's 1917 in Russia. The empire is collapsing, soldiers are deserting, and workers are striking. You've got to decide what kind of economy the new state should build. What's your plan?

answers.text: Hand over factories and land to the workers and peasants.

cons: Elites will fight back hard.
Risk of chaos at first.

answers.text: Keep private business, but with heavy government rules.

cons: Might please no one fully.
Still fragile.

answers.text: Let free markets run and encourage private ownership.

cons: Poor may stay poor.
Could spark new inequality.

answers.text: Form worker cooperatives where people share profits equally.

cons: Not always efficient.
Hard to scale up quickly.

text: It's 1933. You're Franklin D. Roosevelt, stepping into the Great Depression. Millions are jobless, banks have collapsed, and people are losing hope. What's your first big move?

answers.text: Launch huge public works projects to put people back to work.

cons: Costs a lot of government money.

answers.text: Cut taxes and encourage private businesses to hire again.

cons: Unclear if it helps the poorest quickly.

answers.text: Focus on stabilizing banks and saving the financial system first.

cons: Doesn't directly help workers immediately.

answers.text: Distribute food and basic needs directly to families.

cons: Doesn't solve unemployment.
Expensive to keep up.

text: It's 1978. You're Deng Xiaoping in China. The country is poor after years of strict central control. People want change. How do you open the economy?

answers.text: Allow farmers to sell extra crops in open markets.

cons: Moves away from strict equality.

answers.text: Stick to full state control of farming and industry.

cons: Risk of shortages and low productivity.

answers.text: Invite foreign companies to set up in special zones.

pros: Brings in new jobs and technology.
cons: Foreigners may gain too much influence.

answers.text: Encourage village-run businesses that are partly private, partly collective.

cons: Hard to manage fairly across regions.

text: It's 2015. You're Prime Minister of Greece. The country is broke, protests are everywhere, and international lenders are demanding tough choices. How do you respond?

answers.text: Agree to big spending cuts so you can keep getting bailout money.

cons: Harsh pain for workers and families.

answers.text: Refuse harsh cuts and push for debt forgiveness.

cons: Risk of being cut off from funds.

answers.text: Exit the euro and print your own national currency.

pros: Total control over your money system.
cons: Massive chaos in the short term.

answers.text: Make smaller reforms and try to buy time.

cons: Doesn't fix the core crisis.

text: You are a young East German official in 1989. The Berlin Wall is crumbling, and thousands are demanding freedom to travel and speak openly. Do you open the gates or try to keep order?

answers.text: Keep the wall shut tight and call in more guards to hold the line.

pros: Maintains strict control in the short term.
cons: People may revolt harder, risking chaos and violence.

answers.text: Quietly open some checkpoints to let people through without a big announcement.

pros: Eases some pressure without losing full control.
cons: Still keeps people under watch, could anger both sides.

answers.text: Throw open the gates, let people celebrate, and end the wall once and for all.

pros: Freedom and unity are restored, history changes forever.
cons: Loss of control over the system you serve.

answers.text: Delay, make excuses, and hope someone else decides for you.

pros: Buys you time in a tense moment.
cons: You risk looking weak or clueless as events spiral.

text: You are in South Africa in 1990. Apartheid is being challenged everywhere. Nelson Mandela has just been released. Do you push for big reforms or hold on to the old system?

answers.text: Keep apartheid alive and crack down harder on protests.

pros: Keeps the old guard in power a little longer.
cons: World pressure and local anger will explode.

answers.text: Make small, careful changes while keeping some restrictions.

pros: Tries to calm people without losing all control.
cons: Neither side is satisfied, tensions continue.

answers.text: Go all-in: end apartheid, allow free elections, and open society fully.

pros: Freedom and equal rights finally arrive.
cons: Old leaders lose influence, and transition may be rocky.

answers.text: Step aside and let others figure it out while you protect yourself.

cons: Seen as cowardly in a historic moment.

text: It's Beijing, 1989. Thousands of students gather in Tiananmen Square asking for more freedom. As a leader, do you crack down or open up?

answers.text: Send in the army to crush the protests and restore order by force.

pros: Keeps firm control of the system.
cons: Brutal repression leaves lasting scars and global outrage.

answers.text: Meet with the students, listen, but only offer mild reforms.

pros: Reduces tension without giving too much away.
cons: Doesn't satisfy protesters; unrest may continue.

answers.text: Allow free speech rallies, loosen restrictions, and promise elections.

pros: Opens the door to freedom and reform.
cons: Loss of control, risks of instability and backlash from hardliners.

answers.text: Do nothing and hope the crowds lose steam on their own.

pros: Avoids direct conflict for the moment.
cons: Could look weak, unrest may grow worse.

text: It's America, 1964. Civil rights activists are marching, and Congress is debating the Civil Rights Act. Do you support it or resist?

answers.text: Block the Civil Rights Act, keeping segregation alive.

cons: Deepens injustice, sparks national conflict.

answers.text: Support some changes, but keep certain restrictions.

pros: Tries to calm both sides a little.
cons: Neither side is happy; tensions remain high.

answers.text: Support the Act fully: end segregation and guarantee equal rights.

pros: Major step toward justice and equality.
cons: Strong pushback from powerful groups who oppose change.

answers.text: Stay quiet, dodge the vote, and let history move without you.

cons: Seen as cowardly or complicit in injustice.

text: It's Iran, 1979. The Shah is gone, and people are fighting over what the new system should look like. Do you back strict religious rule, or a more open society?

answers.text: Support strict religious leaders and ban Western influence.

pros: Unites supporters under a strong moral code.
cons: Limits freedoms, creates lasting divisions.

answers.text: Support some religious rules but allow limited freedoms.

cons: Neither conservatives nor liberals are fully happy.

answers.text: Support a secular democracy where people can choose freely.

cons: Seen as betrayal by strict religious groups.

answers.text: Stay neutral and let others battle it out.

cons: History moves on without your voice.

text: It's 1941. You lead a neutral country. Hitler's Germany is conquering Europe, and your neighbors are begging for help. What do you do?

answers.text: Stay completely neutral — this isn't your war.

pros: Keeps your people safe from direct conflict.
cons: Allows evil to spread unchecked; you'll be judged by history.

answers.text: Send weapons and supplies but no soldiers.

pros: Helps the cause without full commitment.
cons: Half-measures may not be enough; you're still at risk.

answers.text: Join the fight fully — send troops and declare war.

pros: Stops tyranny, saves lives, upholds justice.
cons: Your soldiers will die; your economy will suffer.

answers.text: Try to negotiate peace between all sides.

pros: Could save millions if it works.
cons: Unlikely to succeed; tyrants rarely negotiate in good faith.

text: It's 2013. Syria is in civil war, chemical weapons have been used, and civilians are dying. Your country has the power to intervene. What do you do?

answers.text: Launch military strikes to stop the atrocities.

pros: Protects innocent lives, upholds international law.
cons: Risk of wider war, unintended consequences, your soldiers at risk.

answers.text: Provide humanitarian aid and shelter refugees, but no military action.

cons: Doesn't stop the killing at its source.

answers.text: Stay out completely — it's not your country's problem.

pros: No risk to your troops or resources.
cons: Allows mass atrocities to continue unchecked.

answers.text: Work through the UN to organize an international coalition response.

cons: Slow process, may be blocked by rival powers.

text: Your country is negotiating a major trade deal. It will lower prices for consumers but could cost jobs in some industries. What's your position?

answers.text: Sign the deal — free trade benefits everyone in the long run.

pros: Lower prices, more choices, stronger global ties.
cons: Some workers lose jobs, communities suffer short-term pain.

answers.text: Sign it but with protections for vulnerable industries.

cons: Complicated, may not satisfy either side fully.

answers.text: Reject the deal — protect our workers and industries first.

pros: Saves jobs now, shows loyalty to workers.
cons: Higher prices, isolation, retaliation from partners.

answers.text: Delay and study it more carefully before deciding.

pros: Buys time to understand all impacts.
cons: Looks indecisive, trading partners may lose patience.

text: At a global climate summit, wealthy nations are asked to pay billions to help poorer countries adapt to climate change. Your country is wealthy. What do you do?

answers.text: Contribute generously — this is a global crisis requiring global cooperation.

pros: Builds goodwill, addresses shared threat, morally right.
cons: Taxpayers bear the cost, no guarantee funds are used well.

answers.text: Contribute something but make sure other rich nations pay their share too.

cons: Negotiations may stall if others don't agree.

answers.text: Refuse — your country should focus on its own problems first.

pros: Keep resources at home, no foreign obligations.
cons: Damages global relationships, climate crisis worsens.

answers.text: Offer technical help and expertise instead of cash.

pros: Provides value without direct financial cost.
cons: May not be what's needed most; seen as stingy.

text: It's 2008. NATO is considering expanding to include countries on Russia's border. Russia strongly opposes this. You're a NATO leader. What's your stance?

answers.text: Expand NATO — these countries deserve protection and have the right to choose.

pros: Strengthens alliance, protects democracies, upholds sovereignty.
cons: Provokes Russia, increases tension, risk of conflict.

answers.text: Offer partnership but not full membership to avoid provoking Russia.

pros: Middle ground, maintains some cooperation with Russia.
cons: Leaves countries vulnerable, may satisfy no one.

answers.text: Reject expansion — respect Russia's security concerns.

cons: Abandons allies, appeases aggression, weakens NATO credibility.

answers.text: Freeze expansion talks and focus on dialogue with Russia.

pros: Gives diplomacy a chance, buys time.
cons: May embolden Russia, leaves applicants in limbo.
